en: That is why the community was never only yours. It exists inside an environment another company maintains, adjusts and can change at any time, with rules you accepted but did not write.
<1>3</1> Is every community what it seems?
Not every one. Today community building is sold as a marketing strategy, and the network encourages those who create and run groups, because engagement is its product.

There are also communities set up to sell, with fake profiles, bought likes and ordered enthusiasm. The network defines what looks popular and what looks trustworthy, and profits from both, the real one and the facade.
<1>4</1> Why did your posts start reaching fewer people?

One day reach drops. The same posts, made with the same care, start reaching a fraction of the people. You do not know whether it was a new rule, a silent punishment or a ranking criterion that changed.
That is the problem. The drop never even becomes something you can check or challenge, and often the punishment is not expulsion but demotion.
The change of rule, the lowering of reach or the suspension do not even become a verifiable and disputable object within the system itself.<1>p. 381</1>
<1>5</1> And when the whole group disappears?

A generic message arrives about a breach of the community standards. The appeal comes back with another generic message, or does not come back. Sometimes the takedown comes from mass false reports, made by people who wanted the group offline.
The network can punish. What it cannot do is punish without a verifiable reason, without consistency from one decision to the next and without a real path of defence.
<1>6</1> What went away with the group?
The people went, the years of conversation, the files, the reputation you built and the place you held there. For those who earned money from the community, the income went too.
Leaving was never free, and being thrown out costs even more. Whoever loses the group loses the very ability to take part in a community that only existed inside that environment.

Leaving means abandoning history, reputation, library, items, progression, emotional investments, networks of sociability and, in certain cases, the very ability to take part in communities that organise themselves within that ecosystem.<1>p. 217</1>

You can demand that the network state which rule it applied and for what concrete reason, offer a path of challenge that works and preserve the group's records. When the removal has no verifiable reason, review and restoration can be requested.

If you used the community to earn money, the case can proceed under consumer law or, when it does not reach, under the Civil Code, with more care over proof. What weighs is your real dependence on the network, and not the name the contract gives the relationship.

In 2025, administrators reported losing all the groups they ran on Facebook at once, with accusations that did not match the content. Meta confirmed a technical error affecting the groups and said it was working to fix it, without explaining the cause of the suspensions.

Before that, in 2019, a meme group with almost 500 thousand members was taken down after mass false reports and only came back after the public outcry. And in 2018 the network itself announced the removal of groups and pages in Brazil that bought and sold reactions and followers, facade engagement.

You work through an app. Who decides how much you earn tomorrow? · Follow the ride · Lex Plataformae
Follow the ride
<1>You work through an app.</1> <2>Who decides how much you earn tomorrow?</2>
You do deliveries or rides through the app and were told you are free to work when, how and where you want. Even so, calls decreased, earnings fell or the account was blocked without explanation.
This path follows your ride, from the moment you turn on the app to the day of the block, and ends with what you can demand.
<1>1</1> What does the app really supply?

It looks as if it only pays per ride or delivery. But what it supplies is the very place where your work becomes possible, with the demand, the calls, the rating, the priority and the rules for staying there.
Without that place, you do not work. That is why changes to it weigh so much.
<1>2</1> Are you really free?
The contract says so. You switch on and off when you want. But in day-to-day practice, the app measures you all the time and decides what reaches your screen.
Freedom is on paper, and control is in operation.
<1>3</1> Who controls the calls?
The app. It distributes calls, calculates earnings, decides priority and sends alerts, incentives and performance notices. These messages are not just information, because they steer what you do.
You cannot check the criteria. You only see the result at the end of the day.
<1>4</1> Why did earnings fall if you worked the same?

Because the rule may have changed. Fare, bonus, area, distribution criterion and the weight of ratings change without clear notice. The account stays active, the name is still partnership, but what you earned shrinks.
That drop is not just a natural risk of the activity when it comes from a change nobody explained.
<1>5</1> And when the block arrives?
The account is suspended or deactivated, and the answer is a generic message about a breach of the terms. The path to defend yourself goes round in circles, and meanwhile the income stops.
The app can drop partners. What it cannot do is do so without a verifiable reason and without a real chance of defence.
<1>6</1> Are you protected?

You are, but the path depends on the case. Consumer law can reach those who use the app to earn an income, when it concentrates control over your permanence, your visibility and your chance to challenge. When it does not reach, the Civil Code applies, with more care over proof.
None of this decides whether there is an employment relationship. What is examined is the environment the app supplies and the way it is governed.

You can demand that the app keep and show your account records, explain the concrete reason for the block, review the restriction and give clarity about the criteria that define calls and earnings. This does not require opening the whole system.
Keep the ride history, the statements, the ratings and every message from the app. A lawyer or the Public Defender's Office can help ask the company to show what only it holds.

Many times. In 2025, the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld iFood's conviction in a blocking case. The courier had his profile blocked, supposedly for recording above-average earnings, and received only generic messages, with no proof of breach. In other cases, couriers banned without notice had their accounts reactivated and were compensated, and a judge found the evidence presented by the company weak.
